blogDescription: A clear, neighborhood-level look at how single-family homes and condos are behaving across Greater Portland. This week we focus on where markets are fastest, where buyers have more room to negotiate, and the big condo versus detached-home differences.
blogIntroduction:
Across Greater Portland the single-family market and the condo market are acting like two different markets. Metro-area single-family homes show about 2.5 months of inventory, a pending-to-active ratio around 28.3%, and average days on market for sold properties near 43 days. That combination points to a generally faster pace for detached homes across many neighborhoods.
Condos are slower-moving by comparison. The metro condominium inventory is about 6.9 months, with a pending-to-active ratio near 13.9% and average days on market around 85 days. That usually means more choices and more time for buyers and sellers to negotiate on those property types.
competitiveMarketsIntro: When months of inventory is low, pending activity is strong and days on market are short, listings tend to sell faster and with less time for buyer decision-making. For example, Northeast Portland is one of the tightest single-family markets at about 1.5 months of inventory, a pending-to-active ratio above 37%, and average days on market around 28 days. Expect these neighborhoods to move quickly, with higher buyer demand and fewer active choices at any given moment.
buyerOpportunityIntro: Areas showing higher months of inventory and longer marketing times generally give buyers more flexibility. Columbia County and parts of Yamhill and Marion counties each have more than four months of inventory and average days on market measured in multiple weeks. In those areas buyers can expect more time to compare homes, negotiate on terms, and consider contingencies.
condoMarketIntro: Condominiums are behaving differently than detached homes in many parts of the metro. Several condo markets are showing five to ten months of inventory and average marketing times that are often well over two months. That means more choices and slower pace, especially in places like North Portland where condo inventory and days on market are particularly high.
condoComparisonAnalysis: The gap between single-family and condo conditions is large in many neighborhoods. Take North Portland: single-family inventory is about 1.6 months with roughly 29 days on market, while condos sit near 9.8 months and about 112 days on market. Across multiple areas the pattern repeats: higher condo inventory, lower condo pending activity, and longer condo marketing times compared with detached homes. For buyers that can mean less competition for condos, and for sellers it means pricing and presentation matter more for condo listings.
buyerTakeaways: If you are shopping for a single-family home in the hottest neighborhoods, be prepared for a faster process. Listings in places like Northeast and North Portland are moving in under a month, so mortgage pre-approval and quick decision-making help.
Condo buyers will generally find more choices and more time to evaluate options. In several areas condo months of inventory exceed seven months, which can translate to more negotiating room.

If you want more buyer leverage, look in higher-inventory single-family areas such as Columbia County, Yamhill County or Marion County, where months of inventory are above four and average days on market are longer.
Balance timing and budget: higher-priced single-family pockets like Lake Oswego/West Linn still show multi-month inventory, so price and condition will drive interest even at the top end.
Track the specific neighborhood and property type you care about. Metro averages hide big local differences in pace and inventory.
sellerTakeaways: Sellers of single-family homes in tight markets should expect faster showings and shorter marketing windows, so have plans for staging, photography and showing logistics ready.
Condo sellers should anticipate longer marketing times and may need sharper pricing, updated presentation or incentives to stand out, especially where condo inventory is high.
In neighborhoods with multi-month inventory, be realistic about pricing and time on market. Small improvements and a clear marketing plan matter more where buyers have more choices.
High-demand pockets like Northeast and North Portland can still command quick transactions, so sellers there benefit from timing and readiness.
Work with an agent who can size up whether your neighborhood behaves like a faster-moving single-family market or a slower condo market, and plan your pricing and timing accordingly.
closing: Portland is not one housing market. Buyers and sellers should look at their specific neighborhood, property type and price range to understand real timelines and leverage.
